readerTitle: Four decisions behind a breakfast subscription
caseNote: 가상 사례 (오피스 케이터링을 하는 베이커리 카페, B2B 고객) · 하나의 이야기로 이어지는 시뮬레이션 · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 구독 전환은 한 번의 결정이 아니라 누구에게, 어떻게 청구하고, 왜 떠나는지 묻고, 어떻게 함께 커갈지를 정하는 네 가지 결정의 연속이다.
misconception: 매출이 들쭉날쭉하면 모든 고객을 구독으로 바꾸기만 하면 안정된다.

sources.text: 반복 매출, 유지율, 확장 매출, 월간·연간 결제에 관한 표준 사업 모델 개념
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 고객 수 일관성: 전체 오피스 25곳 = 매주 주문 12곳 + 가끔 주문 13곳. 구독 가입 10곳(연간 3곳, 월간 7곳), 3개월 후 2곳 해지, 이후 1곳이 작은 사이즈로 복귀해 6개월 후 9곳.
유지율 계산: 3개월마다 10곳 중 2곳(20%)이 떠나면 1년 후 남는 비율은 0.8^4 ≈ 0.41, 즉 절반 이상(약 59%)을 잃습니다. 카드에는 "more than half"로 적었습니다.
주당 $90, 연간 선결제 10% 할인, 대행사 비용 $500은 모두 가상 수치입니다. 실제 계산에는 쓰이지 않습니다.

cards.title: Four decisions behind a breakfast subscription
body: Lena runs a bakery-café that also delivers breakfast platters to 25 local offices. Some order every week. Others order twice a year.
Her revenue swings from month to month, so she never knows how much flour to buy or how many bakers to schedule. A subscription looks like the fix. For the next four cards, you make her calls.

image.label: Baker packing breakfast platters for office delivery
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 이른 아침 베이커리 주방에서 제빵사가 크루아상과 과일이 담긴 플래터를 배달 상자에 담는 장면. 벽에 달력이 붙어 있고 주마다 주문 수가 들쭉날쭉하게 적혀 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Who gets the subscription?
body: Twelve offices order almost every week. The other 13 order only for meetings and events.
Lena plans a weekly platter subscription at $90 a week. Who should she offer it to?

options.text: All 25 offices, and stop taking one-off orders
options.feedback: Simple to run, but the 13 occasional offices would pay for weeks they don't need. Most refuse, and some take their event orders elsewhere.

options.text: The 12 weekly offices, and keep one-off catering for the rest
options.feedback: The subscription matches a need that already repeats. The occasional offices keep buying the way that suits them.

options.text: All 25, with a big launch discount to get everyone in
options.feedback: The sign-up list looks great. But the discount goes to weekly offices who'd pay anyway, and occasional ones cancel once they notice the unused weeks.

cards.title: How should offices pay?
body: Say you offered it to the 12 weekly offices. Now pick the terms.
Office managers usually need a boss's sign-off for big commitments.

options.text: Annual contract only, paid up front, 10% off
options.feedback: Lots of cash early if offices sign. But few managers can approve a full year with a new service, so only a handful say yes.

options.text: Monthly with one month's notice to cancel, plus an optional annual prepay at 10% off
options.feedback: Easy to say yes, with a reward for those ready to commit. In this story, 10 of the 12 sign up, and 3 choose annual.

options.text: Monthly, cancel any time, no annual option
options.feedback: Easy to say yes, but nobody is rewarded for committing, and every office can walk away the day after a bad delivery.

cards.title: Two offices cancel.
body: Say you chose flexible monthly billing. Three months in, 2 of the 10 offices have cancelled.
A marketing agency offers to find new office clients for $500. What do you do?

options.text: Hire the agency and replace the two offices
options.feedback: It refills the list, but if the reason they left stays, new offices leave too. Losing 2 in 10 every three months means losing more than half your subscribers in a year.

options.text: Call the two who left, and the eight who stayed, to ask what isn't working
options.feedback: Both say the same thing: on work-from-home days the platter is too big and food goes to waste. Several who stayed had the same worry. That's fixable.

options.text: Add a cancellation fee so offices think twice
options.feedback: Fewer cancellations on paper, but offices feel trapped, complain to other managers, and leave at the first chance.

cards.title: One size doesn't fit everyone.
body: Say you made the calls. Some offices want smaller platters on quiet days.
Meanwhile, one accounting firm has doubled its staff and asks whether Lena could also do lunch on Thursdays.

options.text: Keep one platter at one price to stay simple
options.feedback: Easy to run, but shrinking offices keep cancelling and the growing firm buys lunch somewhere else.

options.text: Offer small, regular and large platters, plus an optional Thursday lunch
options.feedback: Shrinking offices step down instead of leaving. Growing ones spend more, without Lena having to find a single new customer.

options.text: Raise the price for everyone to make up for the lost offices
options.feedback: Revenue rises for a month. Then the most price-sensitive offices leave, which deepens the very problem you just found.

cards.title: What changed for Lena.

breakdown.label: Offices still subscribed
breakdown.detail: 10 signed up, 2 left, 1 came back on a smaller platter

breakdown.label: Offices that spend more
breakdown.detail: A larger platter or the Thursday lunch

breakdown.label: One-off clients kept
breakdown.detail: Still ordering for meetings and events

cards.callout: The biggest gain wasn't extra revenue. It was knowing it in advance: Lena now buys flour and plans shifts a month ahead.
cards.softwareNote: A software company faces the same four calls: which users have a recurring need, monthly versus annual plans, why users churn, and how accounts grow through extra seats or features.

cards.title: A subscription is a promise, every single week.
body: Lena now owes these offices a great platter every week, including the week a baker calls in sick. A bad delivery stings more when customers have paid in advance.
Each month, every office also decides again whether to keep paying. When budgets tighten, managers review **recurring costs** line by line, and nice-to-have services go first.
The switch worked only because these offices already ordered weekly. Without that habit, a subscription just adds a bill.

cards.title: Switching to subscription is four decisions, not one.
body: Each call in this story maps to an idea from this unit:
list: **Who to offer it to:** recurring revenue fits only a need that already repeats (recurring vs one-time revenue)
**How to bill:** monthly lowers the barrier, annual rewards commitment (annual vs monthly)
**Who left and why:** fixing the leak beats refilling the bucket (the math of retention)
**Sizes and add-ons:** existing customers can grow, or shrink, without leaving (expansion revenue)
cards.callout: **Try it today:** list the customers who already buy from you on a regular rhythm. That list, not your whole customer base, is where a subscription could start.
